title: How to Become Someone People Trust (Building Trust Part 3)
author: The Silent Struggle
summary: This essay argues that trust is the invisible driver of career advancement—more than competence or output—and presents a systematic framework for building it as a developable capability rather than a personality trait. Drawing on Charles Feltman's four-component model (sincerity, reliability, competence, and care) and neuroscientist Paul Zak's oxytocin research, the author argues that the most common trust deficit among high-performing mid-level leaders is not incompetence but a 'care deficit': people sense they are instruments of the leader's goals rather than people the leader genuinely cares about. The article organizes trust development into three pillars—self-trust (keeping commitments to yourself as a foundation for keeping them to others), interpersonal trust (day-to-day reliability, active acknowledgment, honest boundary-setting), and institutional trust (consistency under pressure, the most visible form of trust). The most immediately actionable insight is the 'underneath question': after any major deliverable, asking 'What did I contribute that AI couldn't have?' is reframed as the central trust-building diagnostic for leaders in an era when analysis can be automated. The essay also addresses trust repair—why it requires explicit acknowledgment, genuine accountability, and behavioral change over time, rather than just apology.
points: Trust is the decisive career variable: it determines who gets recommended when you're not in the room, who gets defended when decisions come under pressure, and who is given the next opportunity—all of which happen before competence has a chance to be displayed.

The most common trust gap among high performers is the care deficit: people who are sincere, reliable, and competent can still be mistrusted if those around them sense they are instruments of the leader's ambitions rather than people whose interests the leader genuinely holds.

Trust is not a conclusion reached by reasoning but a neurochemical response: oxytocin—the brain's trust signal—is released in response to being seen, being challenged with respect, and being shown vulnerability, which means trust cannot be manufactured through strategy alone.

Self-trust is the foundation: leaders who routinely break commitments to themselves (workouts they skip, reading they abandon) are practicing unreliability that bleeds into how others experience them, even if the connection isn't visible.

Trust repair requires three things done in sequence: explicit acknowledgment of what happened (not minimization), genuine accountability (no deflection), and behavioral change sustained over time—apology alone rarely restores trust and sometimes makes it worse.
quotes: Nobody says I don't trust you in a professional context. Instead, people stay quiet in meetings. They handle things themselves rather than asking for help. They stop advocating for you when you're not in the room. The absence of trust produces a feeling of friction, of distance, of energy that isn't quite converting into results, but it rarely produces a conversation.

Trust is what moves your career. Even more than your competence or your output. When people decide to give you an opportunity, recommend you when you're not present, defend your decisions when they come under pressure — they are acting from a felt sense of trust. Trust is the invisible air in your sails.

Charles Feltman's work identifies four components that, taken together, determine whether another person experiences you as trustworthy: sincerity (you mean what you say), reliability (you do what you say), competence (you can do what you say), and care (the other person believes you have their interests at heart, not just your own agenda).

You can be sincere, reliable, and competent and still be mistrusted, if the people around you sense they are instruments of your goals rather than people you genuinely care about. This is the care deficit, and it is remarkably common among high-performing mid-level leaders who have been rewarded primarily for delivery.

Trust isn't a conclusion people reach by reasoning; it's a response they have to how it feels to be with you. This matters because it means trust is not primarily a strategy. It is the outcome of a practice. And like any practice, it can be trained.

Trust repair requires three things: genuine acknowledgment of what happened, real accountability, and behavioral change that others can observe over time. Apology alone almost never restores trust. In fact, sometimes it makes it worse, because it raises expectations the person then fails to meet.
